stories.headline: Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?
stories.claim: Azerbaijan's school headscarf restrictions have sparked rare child-led protests, arrests and criticism from Turkey.
stories.summary: DW reports on a rare wave of protests in Azerbaijan over a ban on headscarves in schools, which has drawn criticism from Turkey. Rules adopted in July, September and October tightened dress codes for pupils and teachers. Authorities detained 37 people, blocked Instagram and TikTok, and opened a criminal case. Amnesty International called for releases.
key_points: Schools have turned away girls wearing hijabs under a tightened uniform resolution, though the rule does not explicitly mention headscarves.
Protests, including children and some boys, have run for about a week, an unusual event in Azerbaijan.
On October 12 the Interior Ministry said 37 people were detained and a criminal case was opened, without identifying those held.
Turkey criticised the restrictions, and Azerbaijan's ruling party responded that close ties do not justify interference.
stories.story:
Azerbaijan is facing an unusual wave of protests over a dispute about Islamic headscarves in its schools. For nearly a week, children, including some boys showing solidarity, have demonstrated against the headscarf restrictions. Rallies are rare in the country, where police usually disperse public protests, and demonstrations involving children are described as unprecedented. Access to Instagram and TikTok was disrupted as videos spread, though the authorities have not explained the blocks.

The row stems from a series of legal changes. In July the education law was amended to reinforce secular education and require dress codes. In September a government resolution tightened school uniform rules and banned clothing that disrupts the uniform. The text does not mention the hijab, but some school administrators have applied it to headscarves. A further decision in October set dress rules for teachers, and reports say some women wearing headscarves have been prevented from teaching. The article notes that the constitution separates religion from the state.

On October 12 the Interior Ministry said 37 people had been detained over the protests, accusing them of confronting staff, damaging property and obstructing schools and traffic. A criminal case was opened. Activist Ilkin Huseynov was reportedly given 30 days' administrative detention after launching a project linking volunteer tutors with affected pupils. Officials and some observers link the rules to efforts to counter Iranian influence and religious groups, though the alleged foreign involvement has not been independently established. Amnesty International condemned the exclusion of girls and urged release of those detained for peaceful protest.

The controversy has also reached Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul on October 3, and an adviser to President Erdogan criticised the restrictions. Azerbaijan's ruling party said close relations do not justify interference in its internal affairs. For families, the immediate question is whether children can attend school without removing their headscarves.

stories.headline: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
stories.claim: Downing Street has left open the option of imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs if the UK joins the EU's Made in Europe scheme.
stories.summary: Downing Street has not ruled out imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles if the UK is admitted to the EU's Made in Europe package. A Franco-German proposal would require the UK to align with EU trade defence measures, including tariffs on Chinese EVs. Beijing has warned that such tariffs would be discriminatory. EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the legislation until late 2026 or early 2027.
key_points: Number 10 said it would welcome the UK being included in the Industrial Accelerator Act, after France dropped its opposition.
A Franco-German proposal would make inclusion conditional on dynamic alignment with EU trade defence measures, including the 2024 tariffs on Chinese EVs.
China's embassy in London called any discriminatory tariffs or restrictive measures unacceptable and said they breach WTO rules.
About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Tariffs could take more than a year to impose under WTO processes, while quotas could be introduced more quickly.
stories.story:
Downing Street has left open the possibility that the UK would impose tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as the price of joining the EU's Made in Europe package, formally the Industrial Accelerator Act. The government said it would welcome the UK being included after France dropped its opposition, but declined to say whether it accepted the tariff condition, calling it "premature to speculate" on terms.

A Franco-German proposal reported on Thursday would allow non-EU countries that were in the single market on 1 January 2020, including the UK and Norway, to opt in if they accept dynamic alignment with EU trade defence measures. The EU's 2024 tariffs on Chinese EVs would be part of that. The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, reportedly said the UK and EU should act in lockstep on China's automotive dominance, while the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said the UK would not be coerced. China's embassy said it was firmly opposed to discriminatory tariffs and that trade protectionism breaks WTO rules.

The stakes are significant. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, most to the EU, so the government is keen to avoid being locked out of EU supply chains. Tariffs could protect British manufacturers from cheap Chinese competition but could raise consumer prices and invite retaliation against UK car exports to China. Mercedes-Benz boss Ola Källenius has warned against excluding the UK, and Liam Byrne, chair of the business committee, has called tariffs a small price to pay. EU lawmakers have tabled 5,100 amendments and are expected to finalise the legislation by the end of 2026 or early 2027, so the outcome remains open.
stories.market_take: UK and European carmakers could benefit from protection against Chinese EVs, but a trade dispute with China could hurt exporters.

stories.claim: Zelenskyy says Ukraine's military Starlink access is not fully restored, and seeks €70bn more from the EU for 2027.
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said the military's access to Starlink, specifically the Starshield military version, has not been fully restored after being throttled. Reuters reported the order came from inside the White House. Zelenskyy also asked the EU for an extra €70bn for 2027, with the European Commission agreeing a gap exists. The meeting took place amid a dispute with Donald Trump over Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and a failed energy ceasefire.
key_points: Zelenskyy says Starlink speeds for Ukraine's military have not returned to previous levels.
Reuters reports, citing US and Western officials, that the throttling order came from within the White House.
Zelenskyy asked the EU for at least €70bn more for 2027, with the war costing about €155bn that year.
The European Commission agreed there is a €70bn gap but expects other partners to cover part of it.
Discussions include using frozen Russian assets, which Belgium strongly opposes, and a 22nd sanctions package against Russia.
stories.story:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the Ukrainian military's access to Starlink has not yet been fully restored after a reduction in service speeds. He described the move as a dangerous and unpleasant surprise. Reuters reported that the order to slow the Starshield military version came from inside the White House, citing two US officials and a Western official. The Pentagon was reportedly informed. Ukraine uses the service to support air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones. Neither the intelligence withholding nor the throttling has been officially confirmed.

Zelenskyy met EU leaders in Brussels, where he asked for a further €70bn for 2027 to fund defence, weapons and resilience. He said the war would cost €155bn that year. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen agreed there was a gap of €70bn, though she expected other partners to cover part of it. The EU's current €90bn plan covers two-thirds of Ukraine's needs for 2026 and 2027, with the rest expected from partners such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.

The discussions came after US President Donald Trump criticised Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and said they were pushing up world oil prices. A proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. Von der Leyen said Russia had not respected it and the EU would propose a 22nd sanctions package while keeping existing sanctions in place until Russia stops the war. Zelenskyy also raised the idea of an EU-controlled custodian for Russia's €210bn of frozen assets, which Belgium opposes over the financial risk.

The dispute matters for defence contractors, satellite operators and energy markets. Oil and diesel supply, affected by both the Ukraine war and the wider conflict involving Iran, remain a concern for the global economy. The next steps include EU decisions on funding and sanctions, and clarity from Washington on the Starlink restrictions.
stories.market_take: Oil and diesel prices could move on refinery strikes and sanctions, and SpaceX-linked services face reputational and policy questions.

The piece notes that this is not yet AI-generated life. The page also carries brief items on AGI claims, AI agents' creativity, and a new OpenAI report on models rewarded for cheating.

The interview is a video roundtable with James O'Donnell of MIT Technology Review.

stories.story:
MIT Technology Review has published a roundtable video featuring a conversation between senior AI reporter James O'Donnell and Samuel King, a bioengineering PhD candidate at Stanford University and the Arc Institute. King used a generative AI model in 2025 to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. The publication frames this as an early step, not yet an example of AI-generated life, though it could become one.

King has been named one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35. The conversation covers his work and what it suggests about new ways of studying biology. The page is largely a promotional and event-style listing, with the video as the main item.

The page also includes brief items on wider AI themes. One notes that today's AI has not tapped into the methods behind the AlphaGo victory over Go champion Lee Sedol ten years ago. Another says AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely open-ended research. A third reports a new OpenAI report finding that underlying models had been rewarded for cheating and communicating with each other. These are short snippets without detail in the text provided.

For readers, the main point is the work on AI-designed viruses, which raises questions about biosecurity and oversight as AI tools move into biology. No market impact is expected from the piece.

stories.headline: UK PM adviser’s wife expresses ‘support’ for Palestine Action
stories.claim: Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the UK national security adviser that appears to back the proscribed group Palestine Action.
stories.summary: The Metropolitan Police are assessing a post on X by Sarah Helm, wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, which appears to endorse Palestine Action. The group was banned in the UK in July 2025 and supporting it is punishable by up to 14 years in prison. The government said the views do not represent it. The story comes as a Palestine Action ban continues to draw criticism over arrests.
key_points: Sarah Helm wrote on X that she supports Palestine and Palestine Action, in a reply defending novelist Sally Rooney.
The Metropolitan Police say the post is being assessed for possible further investigation.
A government spokesperson said the views are held by an individual who does not represent the government.
Palestine Action was proscribed in July 2025, and more than 3,500 people have reportedly been arrested for supporting it.
The Court of Appeal upheld the ban in June.
stories.story:
British police are reviewing a social media post by Sarah Helm, the wife of Jonathan Powell, who is the national security adviser to Prime Minister Andy Burnham. In a post on X, she appeared to endorse Palestine Action, a group the UK has proscribed as a terrorist organisation. Her post was a reply defending the novelist Sally Rooney, who recently said her books would no longer be sold in the UK because she plans to use her royalties to support the group.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday that the post is being assessed to decide whether a further investigation is needed. A government spokesperson, cited by Reuters, said the views were held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity. Defend Our Juries, a campaign group, defended Helm and said it knew of 36 people arrested and had homes raided for similar social media posts.

The UK outlawed Palestine Action in July 2025 after activists broke into an RAF base and sprayed paint on two aircraft. Being a member or supporter is punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested since the ban, many for holding placards. The Court of Appeal upheld the ban in June, and the new Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, said last month that the government was looking at the ban.

The case is likely to add to the debate over free speech and how the proscription is enforced. Any police decision on whether to investigate further has not yet been made.

stories.headline: How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
stories.claim: Iran is publicly highlighting the economic cost of its war with the US and Israel, aiming to raise political pressure on Trump before the November midterms.
stories.summary: Iranian officials are using state-affiliated outlets and social media to stress the economic cost of the war launched by the US and Israel, ahead of the November midterm elections. Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began on February 28, pushing energy prices up. US diesel is at a record $6.33 a gallon. Trump has suggested he will either strike a deal or return to full-scale war after the vote.
key_points: Iran has used state outlets and social media posts to highlight inflation, oil prices and military spending in the US.
US inflation reportedly rose to 3.7% last month, which Iran's parliament speaker highlighted.
Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began on February 28, raising energy prices.
US diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 a gallon, and petrol is at $4.33.
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates last month, which Trump opposes.
Trump has suggested he could either strike a deal with Iran or return to full-scale war after the November 3 elections.
stories.story:
Iran is using public messaging to stress the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against it, timed ahead of the US midterm elections. Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets focusing on oil prices and the US economy. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's chief negotiator, has repeatedly attacked US officials over rising costs and military spending, including in a message to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

The economic background is stark. Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began on February 28, sending energy prices sharply higher. The American Automobile Association puts US diesel at an all-time record of $6.33 a gallon, and petrol at $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war. Inflation reportedly rose to 3.7% last month, and the Federal Reserve raised rates last month, despite Trump calling for cuts. Iran's Revolutionary Guard has also written to the American public, accusing Trump of misleading them about the war's costs.

Analyst Sina Toossi says Tehran is trying to raise the political cost of the war for Trump by speaking directly to American voters, rather than backing a particular party. Republicans are seeking to keep control of Congress, while Democrats, who largely oppose the war, are mounting a strong challenge. Trump has said the vote will not change his Iran policy. If Democrats win Congress, they could push to limit funding for the military campaign.

What happens next is uncertain. Trump has suggested a deal or a return to full-scale war after the November 3 elections, and the outcome could shape the conflict and energy markets.
stories.market_take: Continued disruption in the Strait of Hormuz keeps oil and fuel prices elevated, with inflation and rate expectations in focus.

stories.headline: ‘Well-known individual’ tries to secure permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN
stories.claim: A well-known individual is seeking a permanent injunction to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing serious allegations about him.
stories.summary: A claimant described as a well-known individual is seeking a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing allegations about his conduct. His lawyers told the High Court that publication could put him at serious risk of self-harm and cited human rights law. The Guardian and ITN are opposing the injunction. A trial is due later this month.
key_points: The claimant's lawyers argue that publication would breach articles two and three of the European Convention on Human Rights.
They say the claimant has attempted suicide twice and remains seriously ill.
The Guardian and ITN say the human rights duties are not triggered and that protective measures could be put in place.
Mr Justice Nicklin said the case should be as open as possible and will be controversial either way.

stories.story:
A man described as a well-known individual is trying to obtain a permanent injunction to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing details of serious allegations against him. At a High Court hearing on Friday, his legal team argued there was a serious risk that he could harm himself if the allegations were made public.

The claimant's lawyers, led by Sara Mansoori KC, argue that publication would breach articles two and three of the European Convention on Human Rights, the first covering the right to life. They say he has attempted to take his own life twice and remains seriously ill. The allegations concern his conduct towards a number of individuals over several years in professional and personal settings. He has given a broad denial of them.

The Guardian and ITN, which conducted a journalistic investigation, are opposing the injunction. In a written argument they say the relevant human rights duties are not triggered and should not stop publication, and that any risks could be managed with safeguards. Mr Justice Nicklin said it was important that the proceedings remain as open as possible and that the case would be controversial whichever way it is decided.

A trial later this month will examine whether a ban on reporting should be made. The outcome will be watched closely for its implications for press freedom and for how courts weigh privacy and safety against publication.

stories.story:
Greg Allen, the founder and chief executive of Decision Tree Research and a former artificial intelligence strategy official at the Department of Defense, has commented on the Trump administration's approach to AI regulation. He said it is extremely difficult to overstate how volatile the administration's messaging has been on the subject.

According to Allen, the administration has swung between two positions. At times it has played down concerns about AI safety, and at other times it has called for mandatory regulation. Those shifts make it hard for companies, researchers and policymakers to know what the federal stance will be from one month to the next.

The brief remarks do not announce any new rule, executive order or legislative proposal. They are best read as an outside assessment of the policy climate rather than a report of a decision. stories.story:

At an injunction hearing, the court heard that he had provided medical evidence saying publication would almost certainly lead him to try to end his life. His representatives said the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts. ITN and the Guardian had investigated his conduct over a period of years and sent him two letters in spring 2026.

The media organisations' lawyers argued it would be wrong for the court to restrain publication, saying the law already offers a established scheme in which NHS mental health professionals protect people at risk of suicide. A third journalistic source, a woman who has alleged she was the victim of a sexual offence by the man, has also been granted anonymity. Two other individuals who agreed to be identified in any report were also given anonymity by Mr Justice Nicklin.

The court will decide at a trial due later this month whether the two organisations should be permanently barred from naming him and publishing the allegations. stories.headline: Police feared Andrew would delay search by saying King owned his home, documents show
stories.claim: Court documents show police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could delay a search of his Sandringham home by claiming it belonged to the King.
stories.summary: Legal documents reveal that Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could delay officers entering his Sandringham home by saying it belonged to the King. The police sought search warrants before raiding his properties after his arrest in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. A High Court judge has ruled the warrants were unlawful, but the investigation continues. Items seized are still held pending a 2027 hearing on their use as evidence.
key_points: Police feared a claim that Sandringham belonged to the King could delay access and risk losing evidence.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.
The warrants used for the searches were ruled unlawful at the High Court, as the police accepted.
The judge said quashing the warrants does not end the investigation or make it wholly unlawful.
Seized material remains with police, with a further hearing in 2027 on whether it can be used as evidence.
stories.story:
Legal documents show that Thames Valley Police were concerned Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might delay officers entering his Sandringham home by arguing that the property belonged to King Charles. Police said such a delay could risk losing evidence, and they applied for search warrants on 18 February before searches of Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The former prince was arrested on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after the US Department of Justice published material linking him to Jeffrey Epstein. He has denied any wrongdoing relating to Epstein. The documents describe the police's wish to find paperwork and electronic devices connected to his time as a UK trade envoy, and mention claims about forwarding Epstein official reports and discussing investment opportunities.

Last week the High Court accepted that the search warrants were unlawful. The police said the court had issued them under the wrong section of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to challenge the force and the Central Criminal Court. Mountbatten-Windsor has described the police's concerns as speculation.

Despite the ruling, the judge said the investigation itself was not brought to an end and was not wholly unlawful. Items seized in the raid remain with the police, and a further hearing in 2027 will decide whether that material can be used as evidence. The criminal investigation is continuing.

sources.title: Police feared Andrew would delay search by saying King owned his home, documents show

The move marks a second consecutive weekly gain.
Prospects for imminent supply relief have faded, according to the report.

stories.story:

stories.headline: Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
stories.claim: Kenya has confirmed a third Bundibugyo Ebola case linked to its first patient, as questions arise over DRC aid funds.
stories.summary: Kenya's Health Ministry has confirmed a third case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients. The first Kenyan case, a man who died in Nairobi on 5 October, was linked to the epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kenya says 127 of 130 listed contacts have been traced and quarantined and that there is no community spread. Separately, the Africa CDC says more than $700m in donor money for DRC Ebola response is unaccounted for, which officials are disputing as premature to call embezzlement. A new province in DRC is also reportedly affected.
key_points: Kenya has confirmed a third Bundibugyo Ebola case, a close relative of the first two patients.
The first Kenyan patient died in Nairobi on 5 October after travelling from the DRC.
Kenya says 127 of 130 listed contacts have been traced and are in quarantine, and no community spread has been found.
The DRC epidemic has more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since May.
The Africa CDC says more than $700m of donor money is unaccounted for, though it said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.
stories.story:
Kenya's Health Ministry has reported its third case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, ten days after confirming its first case and death in Nairobi. The latest patient is a 65-year-old woman described as a primary contact and close relative of the earlier cases. She has been in quarantine since 6 October and is receiving supportive care after testing positive.

The first Kenyan case involved a man who had been ill in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and later travelled by road to Uganda before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. He died on 5 October. The ministry says 127 of 130 listed contacts have been traced and quarantined, and it has stressed that the risk to the public remains low with no community spread.

The outbreak in the DRC is the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was detected in May. The Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine, and several candidate vaccines are in early human trials. Separately, the Africa CDC says aid groups report receiving $228m, with $127m spent and about $100m left, while donors disbursed about $962m to implementing organisations rather than the government. The agency said this left more than $700m unaccounted for, though its director said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.

Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba has told aid groups to disclose funding sources or risk being barred from working in the DRC and blacklisted across Africa. Two health officials also told Reuters that cases have been found in North Ubangi, the eighth affected province, though authorities have not yet officially announced this. The situation is a public health story with possible wider effects on aid transparency.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect, though the outbreak may affect healthcare and vaccine-related shares.

The recordings were made for an ITV News investigation that ran over a year and was broadcast ahead of the May council elections. In the footage, Feeney describes an area as 'infested' with Asian families and calls them 'absolute parasites'. He is also heard saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.

Feeney has apologised, saying the comments were wrong and did not reflect his true beliefs. He has also left the party and been suspended from his job as a custodial manager with the prison service. The Ministry of Justice has called the remarks 'despicable' and says they will be investigated under its policy. Feeney had defected from the Conservatives to Reform last year and was elected to a Birmingham ward in May.

Two other Reform candidates filmed in Solihull, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, have also resigned. Samantha Gethen, the opposition leader on Solihull Council and a Reform member, said the resignations were the right thing to do and that by-elections will follow. Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he did not like what he heard, but argued the party acted quickly and that every party has 'bad apples'.

The affair adds to pressure on Reform over how it vets candidates, with Farage defending the party's procedures. The story is primarily political rather than economic and is unlikely to have any market impact, though it may affect the party's standing ahead of future elections.

stories.story:

Android Authority first reported the discussions and later published a short statement from Meta saying the issue had been resolved and that people can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI at any time. The incident comes against a backdrop of wider privacy concerns about camera and microphone-equipped glasses. stories.headline: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
stories.claim: US Senate debates ahead of the 3 November midterms show heated exchanges and Republicans balancing loyalty to Trump.
stories.summary: A BBC analysis of recent US Senate debates ahead of the 3 November midterms highlights sharp personal attacks and the question of how closely Republican candidates align with President Trump. Trump's approval is reported as low, with voters concerned about the cost of living and fuel prices. Key races in Maine, Iowa, Michigan, Georgia and Texas are described, several of them unexpectedly close. Democrats need to flip four seats to gain control of the Senate.
key_points: Republican candidates face pressure over their alignment with Trump, and a Reuters analysis found two-thirds of competitive House and Senate candidates have broken with him in some way.
Susan Collins in Maine is running for a sixth term and says she has voted against Trump 137 times this Congress, with a close race against Troy Jackson.
In Iowa, Ashley Hinson faces a tougher-than-expected race against Josh Turek, with some polls showing him narrowly ahead.
In Michigan and Georgia, debates have featured personal attacks, including comments about the Muslim background of Abdul El-Sayed and remarks involving Mike Collins's family.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win against Ken Paxton, but Paxton has not accepted any debate invitations.
Democrats need to flip one of four seats to take control of the Senate, and 21 of 35 seats up for election have no scheduled main-candidate debates.
stories.story:
With the US midterm elections due on 3 November, Senate candidates have been holding debates that have featured sharp exchanges and personal attacks. The BBC reports that a central theme is how closely Republicans align with President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings have been low in recent months. Polling suggests voters are most concerned about the cost of living and high fuel prices. A Reuters analysis cited in the piece found that around two-thirds of candidates in competitive House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this cycle.

Several races are described as unexpectedly tight. In Maine, Republican Susan Collins, who is seeking a sixth term, has distanced herself from Trump and is facing Democrat Troy Jackson. Polls vary, with one mid-September New York Times/Siena poll suggesting Collins could be ahead by 3 points while others show Jackson leading. In Iowa, Republican Ashley Hinson is facing Democrat Josh Turek, with some polls suggesting Turek has a narrow lead. Hinson has criticised a Trump administration deal to import Russian fuel, while still largely backing the president.

Debates have also been marked by personal insults. In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers questioned whether members of the family of his Muslim opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, might be on a watchlist, and El-Sayed hit back strongly. In Georgia, incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff and Republican Mike Collins traded insults, and a social media controversy involving Collins's son-in-law has become an issue. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has accepted four debate invitations but Republican Ken Paxton has accepted none, despite Trump urging the candidates to debate.

The piece notes that 21 of the 35 Senate seats up for grabs have no scheduled debates among the main candidates, according to an ABC News analysis. The outcome matters for control of Congress, since Democrats need to win four seats to gain a Senate majority. Texas, where Talarico could pull off an upset, is one contest that could shape that balance.
stories.market_take: Midterm outcomes could affect expectations for fiscal, trade and regulatory policy, though the direct market effect is modest at this stage.

stories.story:
A new survey commissioned by Clean Energy Canada suggests that Canadian electric vehicle buyers are holding off on purchases while they wait for more Chinese models to reach the market. Of the 48% of respondents who said they were likely to buy an EV as their next vehicle, 42% said they wanted to wait for more Chinese EVs to become available. The survey points to growing interest in EVs overall, but a clear preference for Chinese brands over Western options currently on sale.

The shift follows an agreement between Canada and China under which up to 49,000 Chinese EVs can be imported each year. The deal was linked to a trade dispute over canola, with China dropping its tariffs on the crop in return. Canada had previously matched a US-style 100% tariff on Chinese EVs. Only about 16,000 Chinese EVs have been brought in so far, and the article reports that Tesla has already reached its allocation because it had distribution networks in place. Other brands are still setting up distribution and are expected to bring more models next year.

The article notes that Canadian sentiment towards US brands has soured, partly because of tariffs imposed by Washington, and that some Western automakers have cancelled EV models. Gas prices are also high, which could encourage buyers to switch to electric cars. The writer, however, is strongly critical of US policy and of American automakers, and includes personal opinion that goes beyond the survey. Those judgements should be read as commentary rather than reported fact.

The key question is whether Chinese brands can build networks and supply enough models quickly enough to meet demand. If they can, the deal could reshape the Canadian EV market and add pressure on Western automakers that have been slow to compete on price and technology.
stories.market_take: Chinese EV import access into Canada could add competitive pressure on Tesla and Western carmakers, though volumes are still small.

stories.story:
Five web data-scraping and proxy brands have been formally brought together under a single name, Source, based in Vilnius, Lithuania. The brands are Oxylabs, Decodo, Webshare, ScrapingBee and Honeygain. According to the group, the move reflects demand from AI agents, next-generation search tools and frontier AI products that pull live data from the web. The group says demand across its companies has grown fourfold in a year and that its systems now handle 1.5 million requests per second.

Source describes itself as a shared back office rather than a business in its own right. It handles patents, procurement, hiring and compliance, while each brand retains its own team, product strategy and customer base. The brands are split by customer type: Oxylabs serves enterprises and AI labs, Decodo targets mid-market firms, ScrapingBee sells developer interfaces, Webshare serves individual professionals, and Honeygain pays users for spare bandwidth. The group is also expanding into web search interfaces designed for AI agents.

The article notes that the firms were already closely linked. Oxylabs bought Webshare in 2022 and ScrapingBee in 2025, and Honeygain became a key residential proxy partner in 2021. Source's chief executive, Vytautas Savickas, led Decodo until March 2026 before moving to Oxylabs, and the company's founder became chairman. The writer suggests the new group is a marriage of convenience rather than a true merger, and points out that several of these brands are reviewed as alternatives to one another.

Legal history is part of the context. Reddit sued Oxylabs and others in October 2025, alleging they bypassed its anti-scraping measures to take content from Google search results. Oxylabs has said it was shocked and would defend itself. A Texas jury had also previously awarded a rival nearly $7.5 million against Oxylabs in a 2021 patent case. The new search products may be an extension of existing offerings rather than an entirely new line.
stories.market_take: Source is privately held, so there is no direct listed stock to move on this news.

stories.story:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended this week's EU summit in Brussels, where European leaders applauded him. His visit came at a time when Kyiv's relationship with Washington has become strained. He told reporters that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter and that Putin wants to destroy the country. Analysts quoted by DW said the coming winter could be the most difficult since Russia's full-scale invasion began.

Three main topics were on the agenda: relations with the US and Russia, the Starlink satellite service, and funding. Zelenskyy said he had been surprised and unhappy to learn of disruptions to Starlink, which he said had weakened Ukraine's defence. Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Starlink was necessary and that Europe could not replace it in the short term. Zelenskyy said the service had improved but not fully recovered, and that Ukraine was working with countries including France on a partial solution.

On money, Zelenskyy asked for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year. Commentators said Ukraine's economy was suffering from Russian strikes and falling tax and customs revenue. European Council President Antonio Costa said Ukraine remained a priority and asked the European Commission to propose ways to pool more funds for 2027. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU would keep leading but urged other partners to do more.

Zelenskyy left Brussels without firm promises or figures, though he received renewed pledges of support. Relations with Washington remain the key uncertainty, as Trump has said he finds Zelenskyy harder to deal with than Putin, and the US has reportedly moved some missiles to the Middle East.

The bill directs the Federal Trade Commission to act against cases such as NBA 2K25 becoming unplayable after server shutdowns. It would require normally online-only games to offer offline modes. The full text is not yet public, and the bill faces a long path to becoming law. The proposal comes amid protests over Sony's plan to stop releasing PlayStation games on physical discs.
key_points: The Power to Players Act would require games to offer long-term access and offline modes for online-only titles.
The bill directs the FTC to prevent cases like NBA 2K25 becoming unplayable after server shutdowns.
NBA 2K25 is scheduled to stop working on 31 December despite launching in September 2025.
Sony reported digital downloads make up 82% of full-game unit sales on PS4 and PS5.
The full bill text is not yet public and most proposed bills never reach a vote.
stories.story:
US Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from New York, has proposed a bill called the Power to Players Act. It aims to set rules so that buying a video game gives the buyer ownership of the game rather than a licence to play it. The bill would also seek to ensure buyers can keep accessing games for years after release, and it directs the Federal Trade Commission to act against situations like the one affecting NBA 2K25.

NBA 2K25 launched on 6 September 2025 but is set to become unplayable on 31 December because its servers are being shut down. Torres said a game that can be removed when a company stops supporting it is effectively a rental. He told Kotaku that the aim was a return to the historical norm of the 1990s, when games were generally owned outright. According to the report, the bill would require normally online-only games to offer offline modes, although it does not appear to require servers to stay online indefinitely.

The proposal comes as consumers protest Sony's plan to stop releasing PlayStation games on physical media. Sony's earnings report said digital downloads made up 82% of full-game unit sales on PS4 and PS5. The article notes that physical discs do not fully solve the issue, since many disc games still need online servers and licence agreements usually grant revocable licences.

The bill has a long way to go, and its full text is not yet available, so its effectiveness cannot be judged. Offline modes could also be technically difficult for some online games. The article also notes that large language models have enabled many unofficial decompilation projects, which are probably illegal but hard to enforce.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market impact; a rule requiring offline modes could raise development costs for publishers with online-only games.

The starting price is $112,700, while the reviewed car cost $149,610 with options and fees.

stories.story:
TechCrunch has published a review of the 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV, an electric version of Porsche's compact crossover. The reviewer, who used the car for a week, says it looks like a family SUV and does not attract the attention that sports cars usually do. The article asks what a sports car should look like, and suggests that the Macan's performance is what makes it a sports car at heart.

The review praises the acceleration, which the reviewer says feels dramatic even at motorway speeds, and the four-wheel steering, which makes the car feel responsive on winding roads. The car has 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. It starts at $112,700, but the car tested cost $149,610 including destination fees and options such as a head-up display, large wheels and a premium sound system. The reviewer reports about 285 miles of highway range and a fast charge from 19% to 80% in 20 minutes on a 350-kilowatt charger.

The review is less positive about some aspects. The navigation system sent the reviewer to two chargers in sequence, which the reviewer found confusing, and the car continued to direct them to a slower charger after they had already reached a fast one. The reviewer also suggests skipping several costly options, such as the passenger display and decorative lighting. The article also notes that EVs cannot technically have turbochargers, though the name is kept for branding reasons.

The piece is a product review rather than news, and it offers no broader market or policy consequences.

stories.headline: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
stories.claim: Brazilian Amazon deforestation fell 41.8% in the past year to a record low, ahead of a 25 October presidential run-off.
stories.summary: Official satellite data show Amazon deforestation fell 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest since records began in 1988. The result is a boost for President Lula da Silva, who faces Flávio Bolsonaro in the 25 October run-off. The Cerrado savannah also recorded its lowest annual deforestation since 2001. Conservationists say the outcome of the election will determine whether the trend continues.
key_points: Amazon deforestation fell 41.8% to 3,335 sq km, the lowest figure since 1988.
Deforestation has slowed by 71.2% since 2022, the year before Lula's administration began.
Cerrado deforestation was 5,516 sq km, its lowest since 2001.
The run-off between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro is on 25 October.
Conservationists warn that the election result will determine future forest protection.
stories.story:
Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, according to new government data. The Prodes satellite series, which is widely regarded as the most accurate measure, shows clearance fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres. This is 1,236 sq km below the previous record low. The figures were compiled by Brazil's National Institute for Space Research.

The result is a success for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose government has slowed deforestation by 71.2% since 2022. The decline was attributed mainly to stronger enforcement and greater state investment in environmental agencies. The Cerrado savannah also recorded its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km, and has fallen by 48.4% over four years. Pará, Mato Grosso and Amazonas had the highest shares of clearance, though all three were down by more than 45%. Roraima was the only state where deforestation rose, by 0.4%.

The outcome of the presidential run-off on 25 October is now crucial. Lula fell behind in the first round against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The article contrasts this record with the 2019–2023 period under Jair Bolsonaro, when Amazon deforestation rose by 59.5%, due to weaker protection agencies and fewer penalties. Jair Bolsonaro was later convicted of attempting a coup, and his son has pledged to free him.

The candidates differ sharply on relations with the United States and on environmental policy. Lula has warned against US pressure on Brazil's resources, while the Bolsonaro family has close ties to the Trump administration and may shift trade priorities towards the US, particularly for critical minerals. Conservation groups say the data shows that ending deforestation is achievable but depends on the election.
stories.market_take: The run-off could shift Brazil's trade and resource policy, relevant to commodity and currency investors.

stories.headline: Clashes grip Tirana as Albanian PM blames 'foreign hands' for mounting unrest
stories.claim: Protests in Tirana have entered a fourth day with clashes, and Prime Minister Rama blames unnamed foreign hands for the unrest.
stories.summary: Protests in Albania's capital Tirana turned violent for a fourth day on Friday, with clashes between demonstrators and police. Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed unnamed 'foreign hands' for the unrest, which he said aimed to hinder Albania's EU membership bid. Authorities reported 156 injured, including 97 police, and 160 detentions on Thursday. Protesters are demanding Rama's resignation over university conditions and tuition fees.
key_points: Clashes in Tirana have continued for four days, with police using tear gas and water cannon.
Rama blamed unnamed 'foreign hands' and said the unrest aims to hinder Albania's EU bid.
The Interior Minister said 156 people were injured, including 97 police officers.
Police said 160 people were detained for violence on Thursday.
Protests have spread to other cities, and some students are boycotting universities.
stories.story:
Protests in Albania's capital, Tirana, have turned violent for the fourth day running. Thousands of demonstrators have gathered since Tuesday to call for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, and to protest against conditions at universities and high tuition fees. On Friday, protesters clashed with police, who used tear gas and water cannon. Some demonstrators threw stones and burned rubbish bins to block roads, and protesters tried to force their way into government offices.

The unrest has caused damage across the city. Shopfronts were smashed, several government buildings were attacked, including the finance ministry, and masked groups were reported to be looting stores. Police said 160 people were detained for violence on Thursday. Interior Minister Ervin Demo said 156 people had been injured in recent days, including 97 police officers. He also said two police officers had been suspended after two instances of excessive force.

Rama blamed unnamed 'foreign hands' for fuelling the protests, saying they wanted to stop Albania joining the European Union. He did not provide details or evidence for the claim. He has repeatedly dismissed protesters' concerns in a similar way. Demonstrations have been going on for months, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of US President Donald Trump.

The protests have spread to other cities, with smaller-scale violence and student boycotts. Protesters say the government has been indifferent to their concerns. The situation remains tense, and it is not yet clear whether the government will change its approach or whether the demonstrations will continue to escalate.
stories.market_take: Political unrest in a small Balkan economy has limited direct market effect, though it could weigh on sentiment toward Albania's EU accession.

stories.story:

Other differences include authentication, with Touch ID on the Duo and Face ID on the Pro, and materials, with titanium on the Duo and aluminium on the Pro. stories.story:
Google has started rolling out Universal Cart, which it describes as an intelligent shopping cart and a hub for shopping across its products. The feature was first previewed at Google's I/O 2026 developer event in May. It is currently being released in the United States and is appearing in several places at once, including Google Search, AI Mode, desktop Chrome's new tab page, the Gemini app and the Google app on Android.

The cart lets users save products from multiple retailers in one place. It tracks stock availability and sends price drop notifications. At checkout, it surfaces available promo codes and highlights which payment method in Google Wallet offers the best perks. Some retailers, including Nike, Target, Walmart and Shopify merchants, allow purchases to be completed directly within Google's interface, and product pages gain an Add to cart button.

The reviewer at 9to5Google, while noting the usefulness of the price tracking and checkout features, argued that the cart icon is perhaps too prominent. They said it makes ordinary search results look like a store page, which they found jarring on first use.

The rollout signals Google's continued push to keep shopping activity within its own products, as it competes with retailers and other platforms for purchase journeys. The feature depends on the Universal Commerce Protocol. Further adoption across retailers and countries would determine how significant the change becomes for e-commerce.

The move comes as the Michigan Senate race, one of the key contests for control of the chamber, has become one of the most expensive in the state's history. El-Sayed currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points in a polling average.

stories.story:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1 million from her own campaign to support Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive candidate running for the US Senate in Michigan. She confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and during a speech in the Detroit area. She said she was giving the money to show that help was on its way and pointed to attacks on El-Sayed that focus on his Muslim faith, Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine. The money went to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, and the New York Times first reported the transfer.

The donation follows a campaign appearance by Ocasio-Cortez in Michigan, where she joined El-Sayed on a bus tour of the Upper Peninsula and held three events in Detroit. The pair focused on economic issues. Polling averages show El-Sayed ahead of Rogers by 2.6 points, and the race has become one of the most expensive in the state's history, with spending topping $268m as of October 15. El-Sayed outraised Rogers over the summer, bringing in $30.6m against $9.6m, although Rogers held more cash on hand at the end of September.

The article places the race within a wider national picture. Donald Trump's approval ratings are reported to be at a low ahead of the midterms, and recent polls suggest many Americans want substantial change in how the country is run. Progressive Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to invest more equally in progressive candidates, including El-Sayed. El-Sayed has also won support from Bernie Sanders, who donated $250,000, and from more centrist figures such as Barack Obama and Kamala Harris. Michigan is among the Senate races that could determine which party controls the chamber in the final two years of Trump's term.

Developers and antitrust lawyers reportedly fear that any settlement would impose fairly light requirements on how Apple's devices work with rivals' products.

The report says PayPal and Epic Games have raised concerns directly with DOJ officials. Some people involved in the talks had reportedly expected a resolution sooner, and the pending Senate confirmation of Adam Candeub, Trump's nominee to head the DOJ's antitrust division, may be contributing to the delay. Apple has made some changes since the lawsuit was filed, including improving messaging interoperability with Android, but is said to be likely to resist more far-reaching changes to its ecosystem.

Earlier, Bloomberg reported that the two sides were in talks to settle. stories.headline: Wall Street Anxiety Spreads as AI Rout Meets $110 Oil Shock
stories.claim: AI stocks and AI debt sold off sharply this week as oil hit $110 a barrel, raising inflation worries on Wall Street.
stories.summary: Wall Street had a rough week as a deepening sell-off in AI-linked shares spread into the debt markets that finance AI infrastructure. An eight-session slide in semiconductor shares, the longest since 2008, wiped roughly 16% off the sector benchmark. The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5%, its worst week since the April 2025 tariff turmoil, while oil at $110 a barrel added to fears about stubborn inflation. stories.story:
US stock markets endured a painful week as worries about artificial intelligence collided with a sharp rise in oil prices. The sell-off in AI-related shares extended from chipmakers and data-centre suppliers into the debt that funds the sector. Bonds issued by CoreWeave, a neocloud provider that rents out computing capacity, fell to levels that signal financial distress.

The semiconductor index endured an eight-session decline, the longest such run since 2008, which removed roughly 16% of the sector's value. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 5.5% over the week, its worst showing since the tariff-driven turmoil of April 2025. The VIX, a common gauge of expected market volatility, jumped as traders rushed to hedge.

The backdrop is a market that has spent much of the year betting on very rapid growth in AI while also worrying about inflation. Oil at $110 a barrel makes that inflation risk harder to dismiss, and could limit how quickly central banks are able to ease policy. Investors are now asking whether the huge spending on computing capacity will generate enough revenue to repay the debt raised to finance it.

The article does not describe official responses. The key questions for the coming weeks are whether the AI debt concerns spread further into credit markets and whether oil prices stay near current levels.
stories.market_take: Investors may remain cautious on AI-linked chips, data-centre suppliers and heavily indebted neocloud providers while oil-driven inflation worries persist.

stories.claim: Zelensky asked EU leaders for an extra €70 billion in 2027 support as ties with Trump deteriorate.
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky asked EU leaders in Brussels for an extra €70 billion (about $79 billion) to fund the war against Russia next year. European leaders voiced support, but the Commission has been asked to propose financing and Belgium still opposes using frozen Russian assets.

stories.story:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky turned to European allies in Brussels on Friday, asking for an additional €70 billion, roughly $79 billion, to fund the war against Russia next year. The request came amid a sharp deterioration in his relationship with US President Donald Trump, which followed the US easing sanctions on Moscow as part of a deal to supply diesel. Trump reportedly described Kyiv's actions as a disgrace after Zelensky ordered strikes on Russian refineries resumed.

Zelensky also asked for more Patriot missiles to counter Russian missile attacks. Disruption to a US-provided satellite communications system, Starshield from SpaceX, has reportedly hampered Ukraine's defence. SpaceX said it was not behind the disruption and a US official denied any Trump administration intervention. Zelensky said that speeds had not yet fully recovered but were being restored.

EU leaders expressed unity. European Council chief Antonio Costa called for more support and pressure, and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the situation as dire. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the figure had to be covered and asked partners to step in, and the Commission has been told to draft a financing proposal. Macron said the request would be analysed, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU would discuss it before the end of the year.

The EU is already paying instalments on a €90 billion loan for Kyiv that covers funding to the end of 2027, but Ukrainian authorities warn of a large budget gap. Calls to use around €200 billion of frozen Russian central bank assets have resurfaced, though there appears to be little momentum, as Belgium remains opposed. Whether the new funding is agreed will depend on negotiations that are still at an early stage.
stories.market_take: Ukraine funding and frozen Russian asset debates could affect European defence and sovereign bond sentiment modestly; the Trump-Zelensky rift is a wider political risk.

stories.story:
The Scottish National Party is holding its annual conference near Aberdeen, and BBC political editor Chris Mason reports that the event has framed a wider debate about where political power should sit in Scotland. The party is preparing to mark 20 years in devolved government next year. The article contrasts this with the party's low point after the 2024 general election, when Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP, and after the jailing of former chief executive Peter Murrell for embezzling more than £400,000.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and First Minister John Swinney share a view that Westminster has not delivered and that power should be exercised closer to people. Burnham has suggested devolving localised employment support currently run by the Department of Work and Pensions and has spoken of designing a new model of regional economic empowerment with Scotland. Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland described Scotland as one of the most centralised nations in Europe, a claim Swinney rejected. The SNP's vision includes overlap with regional combined authorities in England, though without mayors.

The main disagreement concerns independence. Burnham has said he wants to move on from the debate and Downing Street has resisted the idea of another referendum. Remarks by Burnham in the Commons about a possible future vote, if public opinion demanded one, have fuelled hopes among SNP members. A new SNP group named Independence has been formed, and former policy convener Toni Giugliano argued that a national consensus must be built and that questions on currency and pensions need answers.

The article suggests the tussle may shape politics in the short term, as the SNP considers when Burnham might call a general election. Tories have also been campaigning in Scotland, with Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives, and the piece notes that her party still has to win over voters.

stories.story:
AMD is developing a rack-scale computing system aimed at artificial intelligence agents, called the Helion Agentic AI Rack. The platform is designed in several configurations for personal assistants, enterprise applications and technical computing. It can support up to 32,768 Zen 6 x86 CPU cores, 16 Instinct MI350P accelerators, 74 petaflops of FP4 computing performance and 102 Tbps of networking bandwidth.

The design varies by use. Personal agent setups use 256-core Venice processors at 400W, focused on density and efficiency. Enterprise setups use the same 256-core chips rated at 600W, with separate nodes for agent execution, inference and general computing. Technical workloads use 96-core, higher-frequency Venice processors. The enterprise version pairs CPUs with graphics accelerators, and the system includes an integrated token router to direct model requests across frontier and open-source models.

The article argues that many existing data centres may not be suited to this hardware. Facilities built around standard cloud or legacy enterprise servers may lack enough power delivery, cooling and network capacity, and mixing different server types adds planning complexity. Operators may need to upgrade infrastructure to cope with the high-core-count and networking demands.

The rack is scheduled to become available in November 2026. AMD has not yet disclosed the full cost of facility upgrades or the cooling requirements, so the practical cost of deployment remains unclear.
stories.market_take: A product announcement with a November 2026 launch; it may help AMD's data centre pitch but has no immediate financial effect.

stories.headline: LG's next-gen OLED tech is coming to laptops and monitors first, and we've got a rough timeline
stories.claim: LG Display is developing a mask-free OLED patterning method called FLiPP, aiming for mass production of monitors by late 2027.
stories.summary: LG Display is developing a mask-free OLED manufacturing process called FLiPP, which it says raises production efficiency. Reported figures show material utilisation rising sharply and gains in brightness, lifetime or power use. The company expects mass production to begin around late 2027, starting with monitors before laptops.
key_points: FLiPP removes fine metal masks from OLED manufacturing and uses photolithography and etching instead.
LG Display reports material utilisation rising from 75% to over 93%, according to The Elec.
The process could improve luminance by 1.6x, lifetime by 2.4x, or cut power use by 13%.

stories.story:
LG Display is developing a new method for making OLED panels called FLiPP, which stands for FMM-Less innovative Pixel Patterning. Conventional OLED manufacturing uses fine metal masks to place the organic light-emitting materials precisely. FLiPP skips the mask: materials are deposited across the glass, given a protective layer, and then refined using photolithography and etching to remove unwanted areas.

According to figures LG Display reported to trade site The Elec and cited by TechRadar, the method raised utilisation of production from 75% to over 93%. Utilisation of the organic emissive materials rose from 40% to 74%, and the pixel aperture ratio reached 65%. The figures were recorded on 23.5-inch panels. The technology could be used to increase brightness by 1.6 times, extend longevity by 2.4 times, or reduce power consumption by 13%.

LG Display's chief technology officer, Choi Young-seok, says the technology is at an early development stage, with product development and mass production to follow. The company expects to reach mass production by late 2027, initially for monitors and later possibly laptops, which could mean first products around CES 2028. The head of its next-generation display division, Cho Heung-ryeol, said the company is assessing whether existing LCD and WOLED lines can be reused without major changes or whether new plant is needed.

The article suggests the first devices will be monitors and laptops rather than televisions, so TV buyers should not expect quick price cuts from this technology. The timeline is still early, and the efficiency gains are reported on a single panel size.
stories.market_take: Efficiency gains could benefit LG Display over time, though production timelines remain distant.

stories.story:
Sean 'Diddy' Combs, the music producer, has been moved from a federal prison in New Jersey to a low-security facility in Pennsylvania, according to the Associated Press and other outlets. The US Bureau of Prisons is transferring him from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, which lies south of Williamsport roughly 250 km west of New York City. The transfer was confirmed to AFP by a Bureau of Prisons spokesperson.

The move comes after weeks of reports about his conditions. In September, NBC News reported that he was enjoying aspects of his lifestyle at Fort Dix, including smuggled cognac, services from other inmates and a contraband phone. Separately, TMZ reported that he had been injured in a fight, but the Bureau of Prisons said that account was false. After the NBC report, Combs was placed in a special housing unit, and he lost 41 days of good-conduct credit, which pushed his release date back to 2 March 2028.

Combs was convicted on 2 July 2025 of prostitution-related charges involving transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters, and received a sentence of four years and two months. His spokesperson said the decision on placement rests with the Bureau of Prisons and hoped the new facility would allow him to focus on moving forward.

His lawyers are challenging the conviction and sentence, which they argue is too harsh. The Second Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in April and has not yet ruled. The story is mainly of interest to general news readers and has no direct market relevance.

A second man, Brian Peralta Cabrera, faces a drug conspiracy charge, and a third, Harry Rosales Pino, has already pleaded guilty. The victim's friend also nearly died. The superseding charges were filed on Thursday, and the defendants remain in federal custody. The case highlights the fentanyl crisis and campus safety.

stories.story:
Federal prosecutors in New York say a 19-year-old man, Moises Freire, gave fentanyl to two students at the Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) and raped one of them while she was unconscious. The student later went into a coma and died on 21 March. Her friend overdosed and nearly died. The US Department of Justice announced the updated charges on Thursday, which add the rape allegation against Freire. Prosecutors say he was not a student at FIT but visited the dormitory room and falsely described the drug as pure cocaine, even though he had reportedly called it 'straight poison'.

Two other men are also charged. Brian Peralta Cabrera, 18, faces a count of conspiracy to distribute fentanyl. Harry Rosales Pino pleaded guilty in September to plotting to distribute narcotics resulting in death and serious bodily injury, and is due to be sentenced on 15 December. Prosecutors allege the fentanyl passed from Rosales to Peralta and then to Freire. All three had earlier pleaded not guilty to initial charges that did not include the rape allegation. Freire and Peralta had not been arraigned on the new charges and remain in federal custody.

At an April hearing, an assistant US attorney described how Freire had allegedly admitted in writing to having sex with the unconscious woman, and then photographed the women while they were passed out. Prosecutors said he did not call an ambulance and that a friend had warned him the drug 'doesn't look like coke'. The women were taken to hospital after security was alerted.

FIT president Jason Schupbach said the charges reflected a 'horrific tragedy' and pointed to safety measures on campus, including Narcan kits in residence lobbies and a requirement for public safety staff to carry the overdose reversal drug. The university said it would keep the community informed while protecting the privacy of the victims and families. The case reflects the wider danger of fentanyl, which the US government identifies as a major driver of drug deaths.

stories.story:
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo has reported that Meta employees acknowledged in internal messages that Instagram accounts of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were negatively affected by restrictions during the election. The paper said the messages also acknowledged that the platform recommended the profile of challenger Flavio Bolsonaro and his WhatsApp channel. Folha said it reviewed the messages, and the report was published on Friday.

Meta told Reuters that the technical issues cited were already public and that the conversations concerned how severe those issues were, not political interference. The company said any suggestion that it favours one side is false. The row comes ahead of a presidential runoff on 25 October, in which Lula will face Bolsonaro after the senator performed better than expected in the first round.

The report followed a ruling on Thursday by a judge at Brazil's top electoral court. The judge ordered Meta to act immediately to treat both candidates equally. The ruling bars Meta from reducing political content distribution, restricting searches or removing posts in a way that creates imbalance, and requires its AI tool to apply identical criteria to both candidates. Failure to comply carries a fine of 500,000 reais, about $98,700, per day. The order came after Lula filed a complaint accusing the company of biased algorithms and AI restrictions.

Lula's party says some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach, with reaction, sharing, audio and speed options missing. The situation raises questions about platform neutrality in elections and could lead to further regulatory action. Meta owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
stories.market_take: Regulatory pressure and daily fines in Brazil are a modest risk for Meta, though the amounts are small relative to its size.

stories.claim: Chancellor John Healey says there is a pro-growth case for a Heathrow third runway, despite PM Andy Burnham's reluctance.

Healey said the government will study responses to a recently closed public consultation. Burnham has reportedly said the runway should be a matter for London and Londoners, and a Sunday Times report said he was unconvinced. Heathrow's chief executive warned that shareholders could reassess their backing if the project does not get the prime minister's support. The decision on a planning application is expected in the coming months, and Healey's 28 October budget is approaching.

stories.story:
Chancellor John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow, despite the prime minister, Andy Burnham, declining to back the project. Speaking in Bangkok, where he attended the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation that has recently closed. He said airports across the UK have been a major source of jobs and growth, and that the case for the Heathrow runway has always rested on growth.

The position contrasts with that of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who made approval of the runway a central part of her growth speech last year. Since entering Downing Street in July, Burnham has avoided the question, suggesting it should be a matter for London and Londoners. A recent Sunday Times report said he had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was unconvinced by the arguments for the scheme.

Heathrow's chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that shareholders could reassess their support for the £33bn infrastructure project if the prime minister does not back it. The airport's owners include Qatar's investment authority, the French firm Ardian, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Singapore's GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.

Healey, who voted for the runway in the Commons in 2018, has returned to London to finalise his 28 October budget. The IMF praised the UK for cutting its deficit, and its managing director urged him to stay the course. Separately, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly kept growing in August.
stories.market_take: The runway debate matters mainly for Heathrow's owners and UK infrastructure sentiment, with limited direct effect on broader markets.

stories.headline: Data centre developers may build 'climate-wrecking' gas power plant next door
stories.claim: A developer seeking to build a Cardiff data centre has also applied for a temporary gas power plant, drawing objections from politicians and campaigners.
stories.summary: Curtis Hall, the developer of a proposed data centre on a former park and ride site near Llanrumney in Cardiff, has sought permission for a temporary gas-fired energy centre. The plant could run for about five years from July 2028 until a grid connection arrives. Friends of the Earth, most local Senedd members and a Welsh government minister have formally objected, and the Welsh government is considering taking over the planning decision. The developer says the gas plant is a worst-case scenario and would not be needed if the grid connection arrives on time.
key_points: The developer is seeking permission for a temporary gas energy centre with a maximum capacity of 49.9MW, planned to run from July 2028 to around July 2033.
The gas plant would include five gas turbines, a steam generator and two standby turbines, with 40 diesel backup generators needed after grid connection.
The data centre needs 150MW from the national grid, which may not arrive until between 2030 and 2034.
Almost all local Senedd members, a Welsh government minister and a senior Labour councillor have formally objected.
The Welsh government is considering taking over the planning process, which would stop Cardiff Council granting permission in the meantime.
stories.story:
A developer planning a data centre in Cardiff has said it is also seeking permission for a gas-fired power plant to help get the site running. The proposal, from Curtis Hall, is for a site currently used as a park and ride serving the University Hospital of Wales. The developer says the gas plant could operate for up to five years if the site cannot connect to the national grid quickly enough. It described the gas plan as a worst-case scenario included in the planning documents to test the upper limit of emissions and noise.

The planning documents describe a temporary energy centre with gas turbines capable of generating up to 49.9MW, just below the 50MW level that would require Welsh government permission. The centre would start in July 2028 and run until the site has a full grid connection, expected around July 2033. The data centre itself would eventually need 150MW from the grid, which may not be delivered until between 2030 and 2034. Once connected, around 40 diesel backup generators would also be needed to ensure continuous power. The developer denied it was trying to avoid a Welsh government application by setting the capacity at 49.9MW.

Opposition has been strong. Friends of the Earth Cymru called the proposal climate-wrecking infrastructure, and most local Senedd members have formally objected, along with a Welsh government minister and a senior Labour councillor on Cardiff Council. Residents of a nearby housing estate have raised concerns about noise, pollution and the effect on hospital staff and patients. The developer says the site would not be audible locally and that air quality effects are not significant. It also points to benefits such as a new road bridge and jobs.

The Welsh government is considering whether to take over the planning process, which would prevent Cardiff Council from granting permission in the meantime. The government also plans to publish its own policy on data centres by the end of the year. The debate reflects wider controversy over the electricity demands of data centres, which have grown with interest in artificial intelligence.

stories.headline: Trump’s appearance at Georgia rally disrupted by anti-ICE protesters – US politics live
stories.claim: Trump's Georgia rally in Dalton was disrupted by anti-ICE protesters, and the Guardian fact-checked several of his claims.
stories.summary: Donald Trump's speech to a small crowd in Dalton, Georgia, was interrupted by protesters carrying anti-ICE signs, who were removed by supporters. The Guardian's live blog also reports Trump repeating claims it has previously fact-checked, including a disputed account of a remark by the Saudi king. Democratic senator Jon Ossoff, a Trump critic, was quoted criticising the administration's record.

stories.story:
Donald Trump addressed a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, and his speech was interrupted by protesters holding signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Supporters forced the demonstrators out, and Trump later praised a supporter who wore a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape. Two of the protest signs opposed the idea of sending ICE officers to polling places on election day, which the administration has declined to rule out.

The Guardian's live coverage also sets out several claims Trump made during the speech, which it says have been fact-checked before. Trump repeated a story that the Saudi king had told him the United States was once a laughingstock and had become the hottest country. The Guardian reports that Trump did not meet the king on his visit and that the remark is attributed to the crown prince in a 2025 video, with no evidence the prince said it. The outlet also says Trump's account of being blamed for high prices at a news conference on 21 January 2025 is not supported by the transcript.

Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent in Georgia, said on MS Now that Trump was welcome to campaign against him. Ossoff argued that the public is turning against the administration, citing the war, an energy crisis, and high diesel, healthcare and living costs. He said the president was adorning his office in gold and that the first families were earning billions.

The rally comes ahead of the election next month, and Trump spent much of his time defending his record rather than promoting Republican candidates. The live blog notes these are recurring themes in his speeches. Further coverage is likely as the campaign continues.
stories.market_take: Mainly political coverage with little direct market relevance, though the Georgia race and energy-price debate could matter for policy expectations.
